name: Grenache / Garnacha

lines.s10: Grenache is the warm hearted red of the Mediterranean: ripe strawberry, kirsch and dried thyme, soft in tannin and generous in alcohol.
lines.s20: Grenache is the grape behind Châteauneuf-du-Pape and most reds of the southern Rhône, and Spain, where it began, calls it Garnacha. It gives ripe strawberry, kirsch and dried thyme, with soft tannin and a warm, generous finish.
lines.s45: Grenache needs heat, and it finds it all round the Mediterranean, above all in the southern Rhône and Spain. It tastes of ripe strawberry, raspberry and kirsch, with a little white pepper. The colour is pale, the tannin soft and the alcohol high. It is raised in large old casks and often blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre. The Rhône and Spain tend to be savoury, with dried thyme and rosemary, while Australia is often brighter and fruitier. Pour it with roast lamb, grilled sausages or a slow braise. It most likely began in Aragon, in northern Spain, as Garnacha, and went with that kingdom to Sardinia and southern France.
lines.sale: Grenache tastes of the warm south: ripe strawberry, kirsch and the dried thyme of a hot hillside, with tannin soft enough for anyone. I would pour it with the lamb or a slow braise, as one bottle for the whole table.

glass.lead: Ripe strawberry, raspberry and kirsch with dried thyme and white pepper, pale in colour, soft in tannin and warm with alcohol.

ladder.where: The Sierra de Gredos, Navarra and higher McLaren Vale sites
Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Priorat, Campo de Borja and the Barossa

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity low to medium, tannin low to medium and soft, alcohol high, body medium plus to full.

old.where: Southern Rhône, Roussillon, Spain as Garnacha, Sardinia as Cannonau
old.glass: Tends to be savoury and warm: kirsch, ripe strawberry and dried cherry with thyme, rosemary, white pepper and leather, pale in colour, soft in tannin and high in alcohol. Old vine Priorat and Aragon are typically darker and denser.
old.cellar: Usually the lead in a blend with Syrah, Mourvèdre and Carignan; raised in concrete or large old casks, with little new oak, since Grenache oxidises easily.

new.where: McLaren Vale and the Barossa, California's Central Coast, Washington, the Swartland
new.glass: Typically more openly fruity: raspberry, strawberry jam and red plum, often with a sweet, candied edge and less of the dried thyme and leather. Newer Australian wines, picked earlier, tend to be paler, fresher and perfumed.
new.cellar: Often bottled alone under the grape's name, or as a blend labelled GSM, much of it from old bush vines; newer wines are picked earlier and aged in old oak.

contrast.why: Both worlds grow Grenache in heat, so ripeness differs little. The Old World blends it with firmer grapes, ages it in old casks and names the place. The New World names the grape and bottles it young for its fruit.
contrast.blur: Garnacha from the high Sierra de Gredos is pale, fresh and fragrant, and old vine Barossa blends can be as dense and savoury as a Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
contrast.call: Dried thyme, leather and a savoury, warm finish lean Old World; bright raspberry and candied strawberry with little of either lean New World.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius: a touch cool, to keep the alcohol in check.
service.glass: A wide Burgundy bowl, which gathers the perfume.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; taste a sample before decanting a young Châteauneuf-du-Pape or Priorat.
service.age: Most within five years; Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas and Priorat five to fifteen.

with.dish: Roast lamb with rosemary and garlic
with.why: the wine's own thyme and rosemary meet the herbs
soft tannin and warmth suit a long braise
ripe fruit takes smoke and paprika in its stride
soft tannin and ripe fruit sit easily with smoke

labels.means: The Spanish and the Sardinian names for the same grape.
A southern Rhône place name: a blend from a list of thirteen grapes, with Grenache in the lead.
Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre: the southern Rhône blend, named by its initials in Australia and California.
A southern Rhône village that makes only rosé, deep pink, dry and full, led by Grenache.
A sweet, fortified red from Roussillon, made mostly of Grenache; a match for chocolate.

guest.q: It looks so pale. Is it a light wine?
guest.a: No, and that is the surprise of Grenache. Its thin skins give little colour and soft tannin, but the grape ripens very sweet in the heat, so the wine is full and warm.

guest.q: Is Garnacha the same as Grenache?
guest.a: Yes. Garnacha is the Spanish name, and Spain is most likely where the grape began. Sardinia grows it too, and calls it Cannonau.
No, it is a village in the southern Rhône. Its red is a blend, nearly always led by Grenache, with Syrah and Mourvèdre.

compare.tell: Pinot Noir is as pale but cooler in feel, with higher acidity, lower alcohol and forest floor; Grenache is warmer, with kirsch and dried thyme.
Zinfandel is darker and jammier, with blackberry, a raisin edge and vanilla from oak; Grenache is paler, with kirsch, strawberry and dried thyme.
Nebbiolo is just as pale but far higher in acidity and tannin, with rose and tar; Grenache is soft, low in acidity and warm.

cards.front: Grenache: its Spanish and Sardinian names, and its likely first home?
cards.back: Garnacha in Spain and Cannonau in Sardinia. It most likely began in Aragon, in northern Spain, and spread with the Crown of Aragon to Sardinia and Roussillon.

cards.front: Grenache blind: Old World or New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Dried thyme, rosemary, leather and a savoury, warm finish lean southern Rhône or Spain. Bright raspberry and candied strawberry with little of either lean Australia or California.

cards.front: Why can Grenache be pale in the glass yet high in alcohol?
cards.back: Thin skins give little colour and soft tannin, while the grape needs a long, hot season and builds a great deal of sugar, so the wine is full and warm.

questions.q: Two reds led by Grenache are poured blind. The first smells of kirsch, dried thyme and leather; the second of bright raspberry and candied strawberry, with neither herb nor leather. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Dried thyme, leather and a savoury warmth tend to mark the southern Rhône. Bright, candied raspberry and strawberry with little of either tend to mark Australia, so the reverse order does not fit.

questions.q: A blind red is pale ruby with an orange rim, yet full and warm on the palate, with kirsch, strawberry, dried thyme and white pepper, soft tannin and low acidity. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: A pale colour with high alcohol, soft tannin and low acidity is the mark of Grenache. Pinot Noir is as pale but higher in acidity and lower in alcohol, and Nebbiolo is far more tannic.

questions.q: A guest asks for the Garnacha she enjoyed in Spain, and the list has nothing under that name. Which of these Italian bottles holds the same grape?
questions.exp: Cannonau is the Sardinian name for Grenache, the Garnacha of Spain. Barbera and Montepulciano are grapes of their own, and Chianti Classico is led by Sangiovese.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. TASTE.world reads old, and the entry agrees that the Mediterranean is the grape's home; the New World side is led by South Australia, where old bush vines and a newer, paler style are both on lists.
Say opens on the Court's own gruh-NASH and adds gar-NAH-chah, the Spanish form a guest meets on a label.

The ladder has two rungs and no cool one: the Court's grid reads Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Gigondas as warm, and the grape has no cool home. The Sierra de Gredos, Navarra and the higher sites of McLaren Vale stand as moderate on the strength of altitude; a checker may prefer another word for them.

The Codex's records on Grenache read true and nothing here departs from them. The thirteen grapes of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Tavel as rosé only, Cannonau and the fortified wines of Banyuls and Rasteau are the Codex's own reviewed facts.

The origin in Aragon is the Rhône wine body's own statement and the common view; some pages argue for Sardinia, so every line says most likely. The spread with the Crown of Aragon stands on two trade pages read through search.

The Rhône wine body classes Grenache noir as intermediate in ripening, so the entry does not call it late ripening; it says the grape needs heat and a long, hot season, which both that page and the reference works support.
Thin skins, pale colour and easy oxidation stand on The Oxford Companion to Wine, cited by its title; the search results did not show the passage itself.

The newer Australian style, picked earlier and paler, stands on Wine Australia and several trade pages; one trade page calls the claim of lightness well worn, so the contrast keeps the riper, sweeter fruited style as the typical one and the newer style as a second sentence.
The Creole dish is gumbo with smoked sausage: soft tannin and ripe fruit suit smoke and a dark roux. High alcohol can sharpen chilli heat, so the pairing assumes a gumbo that is smoky more than hot.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
